claim: Cerebellar dysfunction leads to postural instability.
source: Cerebellar dysfunction leads to postural instability.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: The Tg(aldoca:TRPV1-tagRFP) line expresses rat TRPV1 exclusively in all cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: Fish in this line express rat TRPV1, a capsaicin-sensitive non-selective cation channel, exclusively in all cerebellar Purkinje cells (Figure 1A and B; Tanabe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and B showing labeled Purkinje cells and citation to Tanabe et al., 2010.

claim: Endogenous zebrafish TRPV1 channels are insensitive to capsaicin.
source: Endogenous zebrafish TRPV1 channels are insensitive to capsaicin (Gau et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gau et al., 2013.

claim: Low doses of capsaicin can activate sensory and hypothalamic neurons while high doses are excitotoxic.
source: low-doses of capsaicin can activate sensory and hypothalamic neurons while high-doses are excitotoxic (Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: Prolonged exposure to 1 µM capsaicin increased cerebellar activity in TRPV1-expressing cells.
source: Prolonged exposure to a low dose of capsaicin increased cerebellar activity (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). At each timepoint, TRPV1-expressing cells showed increased intensity relative to a pre-capsaicin baseline, while TRPV1-negative cells did not (Figure 1E, 3/6 hr post 1 µM capsaicin: 28%/20%/ TRPV1+ cells F/F0 > 2; 40 cells from 3 fish vs. 0%/0%/ TRPV1- cells F/F0 > 2; 44 cells from 4 fish; activated cells after 6 hr of capsaicin treatment: 0/44 TRPV1- vs. 8/40 TRPV1+; Fisher's exact test: p=0.0018).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing increased fluorescence in TRPV1+ cells and statistical testing.

claim: 1 µM of capsaicin could sporadically activate subsets of Purkinje cells.
source: Different cells showed increased activity at the 3,6, and 9 hr timepoints, and the same cells were differentially active at different timepoints. We interpret this as evidence that 1 µM of capsaicin could sporadically activate subsets of Purkinje cells.
evidence: Based on observation of variable activation patterns across timepoints.

claim: Capsaicin-induced activation is reversible after washout.
source: Relative to baseline, fluorescent intensities increased after 6 hr, as in Figure 1E. Importantly, fluorescence returned to baseline levels after 40 min of washout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, 6h post 1 µM capsaicin: 40.9%/ TRPV1+ cells F/F0 > 2; washout: 0%/ TRPV1+ cells F/F0 > 2; 22 cells from 3 fish; activated cells before 1 µM capsaicin treatment vs. after washout: Fisher's exact test: p=1). We conclude that capsaicin-induced activation is reversible after washout.
evidence: Supported by imaging data showing return to baseline fluorescence after washout.

claim: Exposure to 10 µM capsaicin caused rapid axonal degeneration and cell death.
source: Exposure to high doses of capsaicin caused rapid axonal degeneration and cell death. We developed a protocol for Purkinje cell lesion: Tg(aldoca:TRPV1-tagRFP) larvae (without GCaMP6f) were imaged at 7 dpf, at 8 dpf after 1 hr of 10 µM capsaicin treatment and again at 9 dpf (Figure 1G). Timelapse imaging of the Purkinje cell axons showed rapid degeneration already 15 min after capsaicin treatment started (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by timelapse imaging showing axonal degeneration and cell counts.

claim: Cell numbers rapidly declined after 1 hr of 10 µM capsaicin treatment and did not show signs of recovery at 9 dpf.
source: Cell numbers rapidly declined after 1 hr of 10 µM capsaicin treatment and did not show any signs of recovery at 9 dpf (Figure 1G and H; median [inter-quartile range]; 7 dpf: control 213 [195 – 271] cells vs. pre lesion 282 [255 – 366] cells; 9 dpf: control 218 [201 – 250] cells vs. post lesion 68 [52 – 70] cells; 3 control and 3 lesioned fish).
evidence: Supported by quantification of Purkinje cell numbers before and after capsaicin treatment.

claim: Larval zebrafish locomote in discrete bouts of rapid translation.
source: Larval zebrafish locomote in discrete bouts of rapid translation (Figure 2B, grey lines).
evidence: Supported by behavioral recordings showing discrete swim bouts.

claim: To navigate up/down, fish sequence these bouts while maintaining a nose-up/nose-down pitch.
source: To navigate up/down, fish sequence these bouts while maintaining a nose-up/nose-down pitch (Zhu et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2024.

claim: Fish adopted more nose-down postural angles before dive bouts during activation.
source: Fish adopted more nose-down postural angles before dive bouts with a leftward shift of the distribution of postures before dive bouts (Figure 2K). Average dive bout posture was 24% more negative than in control fish (Figure 2L, median [95% confidence interval]: –16.6° [-16.9 to –16.1°] vs. –20.5° [-20.9 to –20.1°], p-value < 0.001, effect size = 24%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing more negative dive posture angles during activation.

claim: Purkinje cell lesions at 7 dpf did not shift the average posture for dive bouts.
source: Purkinje cell lesions at 7 dpf did not shift the average posture for dive bouts (Figure 2M and N -11.7° [-11.9 to –11.5°] vs. –11.2° [-11.4 to –11.0°], p-value = 0.002, effect size = –4%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing no meaningful change in dive posture angles after lesion at 7 dpf.

claim: Purkinje cell activity is crucial to ensure that posture during climbs and dives is maintained within a normal range.
source: We interpret these data as evidence that Purkinje cell activity is crucial to ensure that posture during climbs and dives is maintained within a normal range.
evidence: Inference based on the observed postural changes after activation and ablation.

claim: The number of Purkinje cells labeled in Tg(aldoca:TRPV1-tagRFP) roughly doubled between 7 and 14 dpf.
source: We observed that the number of Purkinje cells labeled in Tg(aldoca:TRPV1-tagRFP) roughly doubled between 7 and 14 dpf (Figure 3C, median [inter-quartile range] 7 dpf: 282 [255 – 336]; 14 dpf: 662 [591 – 733]).
evidence: Supported by cell counts from confocal imaging at 7 and 14 dpf.

claim: At 14 dpf, loss of Purkinje cells created more widespread behavioral deficits than at 7 dpf.
source: At 14 dpf, the effects of Purkinje cell lesions on postural angles were more widespread than at 7 dpf and also affected dive postures.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of behavioral effects at 7 dpf vs 14 dpf.

claim: Climb bout posture was increased by 20% after Purkinje cell lesion at 14 dpf.
source: Specifically, climb bout posture was increased by 20% after Purkinje cell lesion (median [95% confidence interval]: 14.3° [13.8–14.8°] vs. 17.1° [16.2–17.8°]; p-value < 0.001; effect size: 20%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing increased climb posture angles after lesion at 14 dpf.

claim: After lesion at 14 dpf, dive bout postures were 26% more negative.
source: At 14 dpf we also observed an effect on dive bout postures. After lesion dive bouts postures were 26% more negative (–9.8° [-10.1 to –9.5°] vs. –12.3° [-12.6 to –11.9°]; p-value < 0.001; effect size: 26%).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing more negative dive posture angles after lesion at 14 dpf.

claim: Purkinje cells of the cerebellum play a broader role in postural control at 14 dpf than at younger ages.
source: We conclude that, consistent with morphological growth, Purkinje cells of the cerebellum play a broader role in postural control at 14 dpf than at younger ages.
evidence: Inference based on the more widespread behavioral deficits observed at 14 dpf compared to 7 dpf.

claim: Fin engagement is speed-dependent, with faster bouts producing greater lift for a given axial rotation.
source: Here, we observed that fin engagement is speed-dependent, with faster bouts producing greater lift for a given axial rotation (Figure 4B, left, Spearman's correlation coefficient: 0.2193; p = <0.001; of lift/rotation ratio [mm/deg] versus speed [mm/s] Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of lift/rotation ratio versus speed.

claim: After Purkinje cell ablation at 14 dpf, fish produced less lift than expected when they swam fast.
source: After Purkinje cell ablation, 14 dpf fish produced less lift than expected when they swam fast. We divided swim bouts into three different bins according to their peak speed (slow: 5–7.5 mm/s; medium: 7.5–15 mm/s; fast >15 mm/s) for both control and fish treated with 10 µM capsaicin. We parameterized the relationship between upward rotation and lift by fitting a line to swim bouts for each speed. After capsaicin exposure, the slopes of the medium and fast speed bins were significantly lower (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), reflecting a loss of speed-dependent modulation (median [95% confidence interval]: slope slow: 0.029 [0.028–0.031 mm/°] vs. 0.033 [0.032–0.034 mm/°], p-value = 0.341, effect size: 6%; slope medium: 0.041 [0.040–0.044 mm/°] vs. 0.018 [0.018–0.019 mm/°], p-value <0.001, effect size: –34%; slope fast: 0.068 [0.067–0.071 mm/°] vs. 0.026 [0.026–0.027 mm/°], p-value <0.001, effect size: –62%;).
evidence: Supported by analysis of fin-body coordination at different swim speeds.

claim: Loss of Purkinje cells disrupts the speed-dependent increase in fin-mediated lift in older fish.
source: Our data show that loss of Purkinje cells disrupts the speed-dependent increase in fin-mediated lift in older, and to a lesser degree in younger fish. We interpret this finding as evidence that Purkinje cells are indispensable for normal coordination of the fins and body.
evidence: Inference based on the observed disruption of fin-body coordination after Purkinje cell ablation.

claim: Individual Purkinje cells showed either directionally-tuned or untuned patterns of responses to pitch tilts.
source: Individual Purkinje cells showed either directionally-tuned (Figure 5C, n=18) or untuned (Figure 5D, n=13) patterns of responses.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data during pitch tilt stimuli.

claim: Tuned cells were distributed throughout the lateral cerebellum.
source: Tuned cells were distributed throughout the lateral cerebellum (Figure 5E), and showed a slight preference for nose-down stimuli (12 vs 6, Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by anatomical mapping of recorded cells.

claim: Pooling responses from untuned cells allowed decoding of stimulus direction.
source: While untuned cells did not show overt directional preferences, pooling their responses allowed decoding of stimulus direction. We applied principal component analysis (PCA) to visualize the data and assess whether the trial types even for untuned cells exhibited distinct separation based on their trial identity (nose-up or nose-down). PCA of the integral of the full responses on each trial from untuned neurons showed near-complete segregation of trial types (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis showing segregation of trial types.

claim: Pseudo-populations with more than three untuned cells achieved accurate decoding well above chance levels.
source: Pseudo-populations with more than three cells achieved accurate decoding well above chance levels (determined by shuffling trial identity)(median [inter-quartile range] accuracy: 3/5/7/10/13 cells: 0.78 [0.68–0.91] / 0.88 [0.70–0.88] / 1 [0.84–1] / 1 [0.97–1] / 1 [1 – 1]).
evidence: Supported by support vector machine decoding analysis.

claim: The relative number of tuned cells per fish was comparable between 7 and 14 dpf larvae.
source: The relative number of tuned cells per fish was comparable between 7 and 14 dpf larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; median [inter-quartile range] at 7 dpf: 7 [6–34%]; 14 dpf: 8 [2–19%]; p-value = 0.7763).
evidence: Supported by comparison of tuned cell percentages at 7 and 14 dpf.

claim: The preferred direction of tuned cells was different at 7 and 14 dpf.
source: While most cells were not directionally selective, the preferred direction of tuned cells was different at 7 and 14 dpf: at 7 dpf more Purkinje cells were nose-down tuned (2/31 up/down) but at 14 dpf more cells were nose-up tuned (11/3 up/down Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Fisher's exact test, p-value < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by comparison of tuning directions at 7 and 14 dpf.

claim: Decoding accuracy of untuned cells did not differ between 7 and 14 dpf larvae.
source: We did not observe differences in decoding accuracy between 7 and 14 dpf larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; median [inter-quartile range] 7 dpf: 0.68 [0.63–0.83]; 14 dpf: 0.73 [0.65–0.79]; p-value = 0.9468).
evidence: Supported by comparison of decoding accuracy at 7 and 14 dpf.

claim: Cerebellar Purkinje cells can encode pitch direction both at the single neuron and population levels with similar encoding accuracy in young and older larvae.
source: We conclude that cerebellar Purkinje cells can encode pitch direction both at the single neuron and population levels with similar encoding accuracy in young and older larvae.
evidence: Inference based on the imaging and decoding results at 7 and 14 dpf.

claim: The cerebellum integrates sensory information from vestibular (balance), visual, and proprioceptive systems.
source: The cerebellum integrates sensory information from vestibular (balance), visual, and proprioceptive systems (Ioffe, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ioffe, 2013.

claim: Disruptions to mature cerebellar function lead to instability, unsteady gait and a compromised sense of balance.
source: Disruptions to mature cerebellar function lead to instability, unsteady gait and a compromised sense of balance (Morton et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morton et al., 2010.

claim: Development of the cerebellum coincides with postural maturation.
source: Development of the cerebellum coincides with postural maturation, and early development of the cerebellum has been extensively studied (Sepp et al., 2024, Leto et al., 2016, Beckinghausen and Sillitoe, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sepp et al., 2024, Leto et al., 2016, Beckinghausen and Sillitoe, 2019.

claim: Changes to morphology and activity of Purkinje cells are thought to underlie the gradual refinement of motor control.
source: Notably, changes to morphology and activity of the output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, Purkinje cells, are thought to underlie the gradual refinement of motor control (Beekhof et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beekhof et al., 2021.

claim: The contributions of developing Purkinje cells to postural control remains poorly understood.
source: To date, the contributions of developing Purkinje cells to postural control remains poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Larval zebrafish balance in the pitch axis by timing locomotion to countermand gravity-induced destabilization.
source: For example, larval zebrafish balance in the pitch axis (nose-up/nose-down) by timing locomotion to countermand gravity-induced destabilization (Ehrlich and Schoppik, 2017a, Ehrlich and Schoppik, 2017b) and by coordinated use of paired appendages (fins) and axial musculature (trunk; Ehrlich and Schoppik, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ehrlich and Schoppik, 2017a, 2017b, 2019.

claim: The zebrafish cerebellum shares the same circuit structure as the mammalian cerebellum.
source: Anatomically, the zebrafish cerebellum shares the same circuit structure as the mammalian cerebellum (Hibi and Shimizu, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hibi and Shimizu, 2012.

claim: The zebrafish cerebellum is compartmentalized into regions with distinct response properties and output targets.
source: The zebrafish cerebellum is compartmentalized into regions with distinct response properties and output targets (Hibi and Shimizu, 2012, Heap et al., 2013, Matsui et al., 2014, Harmon et al., 2017, Dorigo et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Multimodal representations were found in both cerebellar granule cells and Purkinje cells.
source: Multimodal representations were found in both cerebellar granule cells (Knogler et al., 2017, Sylvester et al., 2017) and Purkinje cells (Harmon et al., 2017, Chang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Brain-wide imaging studies have established balance-relevant sensitivity in the cerebellum, identifying neurons that encode body angle and velocity.
source: Finally, brain-wide imaging studies have established balance-relevant sensitivity in the cerebellum, identifying neurons that encode body angle and velocity (Migault et al., 2018) and neurons responsive to direct inner-ear stimulation (Favre-Bulle et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Migault et al., 2018 and Favre-Bulle et al., 2018.

claim: The conductance of a TRP channel is ~1000 x that of a channel rhodopsin.
source: Finally, the conductance of a TRP channel is ~1000 x that of a channel rhodopsin (Bernstein et al., 2012) suggesting that even low levels of TRPV1 expression will be biologically effective.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernstein et al., 2012.

claim: Both activation and ablation of Purkinje cells could induce changes in pitch axis posture.
source: Here, we used the TRPV1/capsaicin system to investigate the contribution of cerebellar Purkinje cells to postural behaviors as larval zebrafish swam freely in depth. Both activation and ablation of Purkinje cells could induce changes in pitch axis posture.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Ablation in older larvae resulted in bigger disruptions to posture.
source: Ablation in older larvae resulted in bigger disruptions to posture, allowing inference of the functional consequences of cerebellar development.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Ablation of Purkinje cells in older larvae disrupted the coordination of trunk and paired appendages (fins), impairing vertical navigation.
source: Furthermore, ablation of Purkinje cells in older larvae disrupted the coordination of trunk and paired appendages (fins), impairing vertical navigation.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Pitch-tilt direction can be reliably decoded from patterns of Purkinje cell activity.
source: Finally, we could reliably decode pitch-tilt direction from patterns of Purkinje cell activity.
evidence: Summary statement of the main findings.

claim: This work establishes a clear role for the cerebellum in larval zebrafish postural control, even during the earliest stages of development.
source: Taken together our results establish a clear role for the cerebellum in larval zebrafish postural control, even during the earliest stages of development.
evidence: Summary statement of the main conclusions.

claim: Purkinje cell output is inhibitory.
source: Purkinje cell output is inhibitory (Ito et al., 1964, Ito et al., 1970), Purkinje cells in the lateral cerebellum project to vestibular nuclei (Matsui et al., 2014, Knogler et al., 2019), and Purkinje cells are tonically active (Cerminara and Rawson, 2004, Jadhav et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Purkinje cells in the lateral cerebellum project to vestibular nuclei.
source: Purkinje cell output is inhibitory (Ito et al., 1964, Ito et al., 1970), Purkinje cells in the lateral cerebellum project to vestibular nuclei (Matsui et al., 2014, Knogler et al., 2019), and Purkinje cells are tonically active (Cerminara and Rawson, 2004, Jadhav et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Matsui et al., 2014 and Knogler et al., 2019.

claim: Purkinje cells are tonically active.
source: Purkinje cell output is inhibitory (Ito et al., 1964, Ito et al., 1970), Purkinje cells in the lateral cerebellum project to vestibular nuclei (Matsui et al., 2014, Knogler et al., 2019), and Purkinje cells are tonically active (Cerminara and Rawson, 2004, Jadhav et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cerminara and Rawson, 2004 and Jadhav et al., 2023.

claim: The net effect of Purkinje cell loss would be disinhibition of target nuclei responsible for encoding posture and parameterizing corrective pitch-axis behaviors.
source: We propose that the net effect of Purkinje cell loss would be disinhibition of target nuclei responsible for encoding posture and parameterizing corrective pitch-axis behaviors.
evidence: Inference based on known properties of Purkinje cell output.

claim: Synchronized/precisely timed Purkinje cell output is thought to shape movements.
source: Synchronized/precisely timed Purkinje cell output is thought to shape movements (Heck et al., 2007, Person and Raman, 2011, Person and Raman, 2012, Han et al., 2018, Payne et al., 2019, Nashef et al., 2023), although perhaps not for all behaviors (Herzfeld et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The net effect of 1 µM of capsaicin is ultimately disruptive to Purkinje cell synchrony.
source: Our imaging suggests that the set of Purkinje cells activated at any one moment in time is limited and random. We therefore propose that the net effect of 1 µM of capsaicin is ultimately disruptive to Purkinje cell synchrony, and thus likely disruptive.
evidence: Inference based on imaging observations of stochastic activation.

claim: Population coding requires that multiple Purkinje cells converge onto downstream targets, which is well-established in cerebellar target nuclei.
source: Population coding requires that multiple Purkinje cells converge onto downstream targets, which is well-established in cerebellar target nuclei (Person and Raman, 2011, Heck et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Person and Raman, 2011 and Heck et al., 2013.

claim: In larval zebrafish, Purkinje cells involved in locomotion converge on eurydendroid cells.
source: In larval zebrafish, Purkinje cells involved in locomotion converge on eurydendroid cells; electrophysiological recordings confirm a many-to-one convergence scheme that could similarly support population coding (Harmon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harmon et al., 2017.

claim: Vestibular-sensitive cells are located in the lateral cerebellum.
source: Vestibular-sensitive cells are located in the lateral cerebellum (Migault et al., 2018, Favre-Bulle et al., 2018), which projects to hindbrain regions that contain vestibular nuclei (Hamling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Migault et al., 2018, Favre-Bulle et al., 2018, and Hamling et al., 2015.

claim: TRPV1/capsaicin is a well-validated approach that permits parametric (i.e. dose-dependent) activation/ablation with a single transgenic line.
source: TRPV1/capsaicin is a well-validated approach (Chen et al., 2016) that permits parametric (i.e. dose-dependent) activation/ablation with a single transgenic line.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2016.

claim: TRPV1/capsaicin does not require light, facilitating dissociation of vestibular from visual contributions.
source: It does not require light, facilitating dissociation of vestibular from visual contributions without requiring genetically blind fish as in other studies using excitatory opsins (Schoppik et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on the properties of the TRPV1/capsaicin system.

claim: TRPV1-mediated ablation is rapid and precise, with capsaicin triggering almost instantaneous cell death.
source: In contrast, TRPV1-mediated ablation is rapid and precise, with capsaicin triggering almost instantaneous cell death.
evidence: Supported by the timelapse imaging data showing rapid axonal degeneration.

claim: The cerebellum emerged early in the evolution of vertebrates, when vertebrate life was underwater.
source: The cerebellum emerged early in the evolution of vertebrates, when vertebrate life was underwater.
evidence: Statement about evolutionary history.

claim: This work establishes a new tool to investigate ancient organizing principles of cerebellar function.
source: Our work establishes a new tool to investigate ancient organizing principles of cerebellar function.
evidence: Summary statement of the broader significance of the work.
